name: Social Login (OAuth Aggregator)
description: Design a social login system supporting OAuth providers like Google, GitHub, and Facebook. Covers OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, token exchange, account linking, and session management.

learnSteps.title: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow
learnSteps.description: The client redirects the user to the chosen provider (Google/GitHub). After the user grants consent, the provider redirects back with an authorization code. The client sends this code to the Auth Server, which exchanges it with the provider for an access token and ID token. This server-side exchange prevents token leakage in the browser. The API Gateway rate-limits login attempts to prevent abuse.

learnSteps.title: Token Exchange with Providers
learnSteps.description: The Auth Server calls the provider's token endpoint with the authorization code, client ID, and client secret. Google returns an ID token (JWT with email, name, picture) plus an access token. GitHub returns an access token, requiring a separate /user API call for profile data. The Auth Server normalizes both responses into a unified user profile format before proceeding with account lookup.

learnSteps.title: Account Linking and Creation
learnSteps.description: The Auth Server queries PostgreSQL for an existing user matching the provider's email. If found, it links the OAuth identity to the existing account (supports multiple providers per user). If not found, it creates a new user record with the provider profile. The users table stores provider_id + provider_type as a unique constraint. Refresh tokens from providers are encrypted at rest in the DB.

learnSteps.title: Session Management and Caching
learnSteps.description: After successful authentication, the Auth Server issues its own JWT access token (15 min TTL) and refresh token (7 day TTL). The session is stored in Redis keyed by session ID with the user's profile and permissions. Subsequent API requests validate the JWT signature locally; Redis is only hit for refresh or revocation checks. Logout deletes the Redis entry, instantly invalidating the session across all services.

chaosScenarios.name: Identity Provider Outage
chaosScenarios.description: Google OAuth token endpoint returns errors for all exchange attempts
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: New Google logins fail fast within the upstream timeout. Sessions already issued keep working because JWTs validate locally. Login success rate drops roughly in proportion to Google share of the provider mix; GitHub logins are unaffected.
mitigationSteps: Circuit-break Google calls after consecutive failures so requests fail fast instead of timing out
Show provider-specific outage messaging and steer users to GitHub or other fallback
Do not retry authorization codes — they are single-use; ask the user to restart the flow
Watch the provider status page and close the breaker gradually on recovery

chaosScenarios.name: Session Cache Failure
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Access-token validation is unaffected (local JWT signature checks), but refresh, logout, and revocation checks fail. Users get logged out as 15-minute access tokens expire, and revoked sessions cannot be enforced until Redis recovers.
mitigationSteps: Fail over to the Redis replica
Temporarily fall back to PostgreSQL session lookup for refresh (degraded latency)
Extend the access-token grace window only with explicit security-team approval
Audit and apply the revocation backlog once the cache returns

chaosScenarios.name: Provider Token Endpoint Slowdown
chaosScenarios.description: GitHub token exchange latency rises from ~300ms to 3s+
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: In-flight upstream calls pile up and hold auth-server connection slots; login p99 climbs toward the 15s gateway timeout while Google logins stay fast. Without bulkheading, GitHub slowness starves capacity for every provider.
mitigationSteps: Enforce a 2s upstream timeout; never auto-retry the code exchange POST
Bulkhead per-provider connection pools so GitHub exhaustion cannot starve Google flows
Prioritize session refresh traffic ahead of new interactive logins
Open the GitHub circuit breaker if p99 stays elevated beyond 5 minutes

bottleneckProgression.description: JWT signing, TLS to providers, and token-exchange handling saturate the 6-instance fleet
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Scale instances; cache provider JWKS and OpenID discovery documents to cut per-login work

bottleneckProgression.description: Account lookup and identity-link writes exhaust the 200-connection pool during login surges
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Add a connection pooler and route account lookups to a read replica

bottleneckProgression.description: TLS termination and rate-limit evaluation saturate the gateway as traffic approaches its 20k RPS configuration
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Scale the gateway horizontally and push coarse rate limiting to the edge

expectedIssues.title: Account Takeover via Unverified Email Linking
expectedIssues.description: Auto-linking provider identities by email lets an attacker claim a victim account through a provider that does not verify email ownership
expectedIssues.mitigation: Only auto-link when the provider asserts email_verified; otherwise require authentication to the existing account before linking

expectedIssues.title: Provider Rate Limit Ceilings
expectedIssues.description: GitHub (5k RPS) and Google (10k RPS) quotas cap login bursts from marketing pushes or incident-driven re-login storms below platform capacity
expectedIssues.mitigation: Spread re-auth with jittered token expiry, pre-negotiate quota increases, and queue non-interactive refreshes

expectedIssues.title: Refresh Token Theft and Replay
expectedIssues.description: A stolen refresh token grants up to 7 days of access if undetected
expectedIssues.mitigation: Rotate refresh tokens on every use and revoke the entire session family when reuse is detected

expectedIssues.title: Provider Signing Key Rotation
expectedIssues.description: If provider JWKS are cached too aggressively, ID-token verification fails platform-wide when the provider rotates keys
expectedIssues.mitigation: Honor JWKS cache-control headers and re-fetch on unknown kid before rejecting a token

slaDefinitions.name: Interactive Login Latency
slaDefinitions.penalty: Internal SLO — provider timeout tuning review

metrics.name: login_attempts_total
metrics.description: Login attempts by provider and outcome

steps: Confirm against the provider status page and error signatures in logs
Verify the circuit breaker opened so logins fail fast instead of timing out
Enable the outage banner steering users to healthy providers
After recovery, watch for a re-login surge against provider rate limits
Fail over to the Redis replica and confirm replication health
Enable DB-backed session fallback for refresh traffic
Monitor login latency for the fallback penalty
Apply queued revocations and audit for gaps once Redis returns
Rotate the JWT signing key immediately and publish the new JWKS
Force-expire all refresh tokens, requiring re-authentication
Audit token issuance logs for anomalous grants
Engage the security incident process and preserve evidence

decisions.title: Server-Side Authorization Code Exchange
decisions.context: Provider tokens must never transit the browser, where they can leak via XSS or history
decisions.decision: Clients deliver only the one-time authorization code; the Auth Server holds client secrets and performs the exchange
consequences: Provider tokens and client secrets stay server-side
The Auth Server becomes a hard dependency for every login
PKCE can be layered on for public clients without changing the architecture

decisions.title: First-Party JWTs Instead of Proxying Provider Tokens
decisions.context: Provider tokens differ in format, lifetime, and validation cost
decisions.decision: After exchange, mint a short-lived first-party JWT (15 min) plus refresh token, normalized across providers
consequences: Downstream services validate one token format locally with zero provider calls
Provider-specific quirks (GitHub needing a separate /user call) are isolated in the Auth Server
Session lifetime is decoupled from provider session lifetime

decisions.title: Hybrid Stateless JWT + Redis Session
decisions.context: Pure stateless JWTs cannot be revoked before expiry; pure server-side sessions hit the store on every request
decisions.decision: Local JWT validation for access; Redis consulted only for refresh and revocation
consequences: Steady-state request validation costs no network calls
A revoked session can remain usable up to one access-token TTL
Redis failure degrades refresh and logout, not active sessions

tradeoffs.cost: Revocation takes effect up to 15 minutes late for access tokens already issued

tradeoffs.choice: Normalize providers behind one profile schema
tradeoffs.benefit: Adding a provider never touches downstream services
tradeoffs.cost: Per-provider adapters must be built and maintained

tradeoffs.choice: Accept provider dependency for new logins only
tradeoffs.benefit: Existing sessions survive any provider outage
tradeoffs.cost: New-login availability is capped by the weakest provider

alternatives.name: Hosted Identity (Auth0 / Cognito)
alternatives.description: Outsource the entire OAuth aggregation layer to a managed identity provider
alternatives.prosVsCons: Fastest to ship and professionally audited, but per-MAU pricing scales poorly and account-linking rules are constrained
alternatives.whyNotChosen: At 100k+ concurrent users, per-MAU cost and control over linking logic favored building in-house

alternatives.name: Implicit / Front-Channel Flow
alternatives.description: The provider returns tokens directly to the browser
alternatives.prosVsCons: Removes the server exchange hop, but exposes tokens to the user agent; deprecated by the OAuth 2.0 Security BCP
alternatives.whyNotChosen: A deprecated pattern with well-documented token-leak vectors

alternatives.name: SAML Federation
alternatives.prosVsCons: Strong enterprise IdP support, but XML signature complexity and a poor fit for consumer providers like GitHub
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Target providers are OAuth/OIDC-native consumer identity providers
